content: Mouthwash, also known as mouth rinse, is a product designed to support oral hygiene. Antiseptic and anti-plaque mouth rinses are formulated to kill bacterial plaque, which is responsible for causing dental caries, gingivitis, and halitosis (bad breath). Anti-cavity mouth rinses, on the other hand, often contain fluoride to help protect against tooth decay. However, it is widely accepted that mouthwash is not a substitute for brushing and flossing, which remain essential components of oral care. In situations where commercial mouthwash is unavailable, gargling with plain water is recommended to help remove food particles, sugars, and other debris from the mouth. Mouthwash can also assist in clearing mucus and food particles from deeper areas of the throat. It is worth noting that mouthwashes with high alcohol content or strong flavors may induce coughing when used for this purpose. The earliest documented use of mouth rinsing dates back to approximately 2700 BCE in Chinese medicine, where it was employed to treat gingivitis. During the Greek and Roman eras, mouth rinsing became a common practice among the upper classes following mechanical cleaning of the teeth. Hippocrates, the renowned Greek physician, recommended a mixture of salt, alum, and vinegar for oral care. The Jewish Talmud, written around 1800 years ago, also describes a remedy for gum diseases that included dough water and olive oil. In the 17th century, Anton van Leeuwenhoek, a pioneering microscopist, observed motile microorganisms in dental plaque and water samples. He experimented with vinegar and brandy, discovering that these substances could immobilize or kill microorganisms in water. However, when used as a mouthwash, these solutions failed to eliminate the organisms embedded in dental plaque, as they either did not reach the plaque or were not present long enough to be effective. This limitation persisted until the late 1960s, when Harald Loe, a professor at the Royal Dental College in Aarhus, Denmark, demonstrated that chlorhexidine could effectively prevent dental plaque accumulation. Chlorhexidine's efficacy lies in its strong adherence to oral surfaces, allowing it to remain active for extended periods. Since then, commercial interest in mouthwashes has grown significantly, with many products claiming to reduce plaque buildup, alleviate gingivitis, combat bad breath, and target volatile sulfur compound (VSC)-producing anaerobic bacteria responsible for unpleasant odors and tastes in the mouth. The typical usage of mouthwash involves rinsing the mouth with approximately 20 milliliters (2/3 fluid ounces) of the solution twice daily after brushing. The liquid is swished or gargled for about 30 seconds before being spat out. Some brands include staining agents in the expectorate, allowing users to visualize bacteria and debris. It is generally recommended to wait at least an hour after brushing with toothpaste before using mouthwash, as anionic compounds in toothpaste can deactivate cationic agents in the rinse. The most effective time to use mouthwash is often considered to be before bedtime. Commercial mouthwashes contain a variety of active ingredients, including thymol, eucalyptol, hexetidine, methyl salicylate, menthol, chlorhexidine gluconate, benzalkonium chloride, cetylpyridinium chloride, methylparaben, hydrogen peroxide, domiphen bromide, and sometimes fluoride, enzymes, or calcium. Additional components include water, sweeteners such as sorbitol, sucralose, sodium saccharin, and xylitol, which also acts as a bacterial inhibitor. Many mouthwashes contain alcohol, sometimes up to 20%, which serves as a flavor carrier, provides a bite, and contributes to antibacterial effects. However, alcohol can act as a drying agent, potentially exacerbating chronic bad breath. Alcohol-containing mouthwashes may also lead to false positives on breathalyzer tests and pose a risk of misuse by individuals with alcohol dependency. Concerns have been raised about the potential carcinogenicity of alcohol in mouthwashes, but no conclusive evidence has been found. To maintain freshness after opening, commercial mouthwashes often include preservatives such as sodium benzoate. Many newer formulations are alcohol-free and incorporate odor-eliminating agents like oxidizers and odor-preventing agents such as zinc ion technology to combat bad breath. Homemade saltwater rinses, prepared by dissolving a teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water, are commonly used to treat oral infections, injuries, or post-extraction wounds. Diluted hydrogen peroxide is another frequently used home remedy. It is important to note that many commercial mouthwashes are highly acidic. Individuals with conditions such as heartburn, acid reflux, or acid indigestion should opt for mouthwashes with a neutral pH to avoid irritation.
